chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban ibn Uthman, from al-Fadl ibn Abd al-Malik and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

that a group of people came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so they said: 'A cow of ours overcame us and became unruly against us, so we struck it with the sword.' So he ordered them to eat it.

key_terms.أَمَرَهُمْ بِأَكْلِهَا: He ordered them to eat it — the Prophet's ruling permitting consumption
key_terms.اسْتَصْعَبَتْ: Became difficult/unruly — refused to be controlled for ritual slaughter
key_terms.بِالسَّيْفِ: With the sword — indicating that striking rather than slitting the throat was used
key_terms.غَلَبَتْنَا: It overcame us — the animal resisted normal handling and slaughter

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to eat an animal that was killed by striking with a sword when it could not be properly slaughtered?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) narrates from the Prophet (SAWW) that when a cow became uncontrollable and was killed by striking with a sword rather than proper ritual slaughter (dhabh), the Prophet ruled that it was still permissible to eat. This hadith addresses an emergency situation where the animal could not be slaughtered in the prescribed manner — being struck with a sword on any part of the body suffices as lawful slaughter when the animal is otherwise uncontrollable. This ruling reflects the Islamic jurisprudential principle that necessity makes otherwise restrictive rulings more flexible.
